newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless claims down, hint tight labor market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless claims down, hint tight labor market.

text.p: U.S. jobless claims surprised some on Wall Street on Thursday after the report dropped more than expected, suggesting the country's labor market remains tight, analysts said.
"I think that generally the initial claims series still suggest that the labor market is pretty strong," said David Sloan, senior economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
The US Labor Department said jobless claims fell to 320,000 in the week ended October 19 against a revised 342,000 in the prior week. Wall Street expected claims to drop to 336,000.

Analysts said the numbers were partially influenced by a 20-day long strike of General Motors auto workers in Canada, which forced GM to shut down some GM plants in the U.S. and eventually lay off nearly 20,000 workers.
GM and the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) agreed to settle the strike on Tuesday, October 22, with a new three-year contract.
But analysts said the impact of the strike on this week's jobless report was softer than expected, hinting that next week's figures still might be driven by GM's layoffs.
"A lot of people were expecting larger effects from the General Motors strike from Canada and that did not materialize," said Waldo Best, senior economist at Barclays de Zeote Wedd Government Inc.

"The strike is settled but GM is saying it's going to take 10 days to have big plants back up and running until the parts start flowing from Canada again. So you can still see some effect of the strike into next week," Best said.
Some analysts also paid special attention to the upward revision to 342,000 claims in the week ended October 12 from a first released reading of 340,000.

They said the revision suggests higher-than-expected softness in the labor market earlier in the month, which might prompt some economists on Wall Street to lower their forecasts for the key October non-farm payrolls report.
"That revision says the labor market during the survey week was much softer than we've thought and that's going to cause the Street number on payrolls to move down," Best said.
"I'm already on 177,000 for October payrolls and I might lower my number," Best added. The October employment report is scheduled to be released on November 1.

The U.S. Treasury market staged a bearish reaction to the jobless claims figures, with the benchmark 30-year bond dropping more than 10/32 shortly after the numbers were released to yield 6.85 percent.
"The market was already vulnerable because of the supply and a higher-than-expected jobless claims report just encouraged the market's sell-off," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Earlier in the week, the market took in some $30 billion in fresh two- and five-year Treasury notes during the Treasury's monthly auctions.
